lessons.title: Repair Café Work: Shifts and Supplies
lessons.objective: Learners will understand and correctly use sign up for a shift and runs out of in workplace contexts.

reading.text: At the East Market repair café, volunteers meet at 9 a.m. to prepare shared tools for a free repair session. New volunteers sign up for a shift using the schedule beside the entrance. The shift lead checks each tool and places items that need attention in a labelled tray. If the café runs out of a common part, volunteers record the item and tell the visitor what can be repaired that day. They do not promise a completion time until a technician has inspected the item. At closing, the lead passes on any unfinished requests to the next team. Visitors may wait in the seating area while a repair is in progress.

They do not promise a completion time until a technician has inspected the item.
At closing, the lead passes on any unfinished requests to the next team.
Visitors may wait in the seating area while a repair is in progress.

targets.meaningEn: to register to work during a particular period of time
targets.meaningVi: đăng ký làm một ca làm việc

targets.meaningEn: to have no more of something left because it has all been used
targets.meaningVi: hết sạch, không còn thứ gì đó

exercises.prompt: In sentence s3 'New volunteers sign up for a shift using the schedule beside the entrance,' what does 'sign up for a shift' mean?

options.text: They write their names to register to work during a particular period of time.
options.explanation: This is correct because it paraphrases registering to work during a particular period.

options.text: They arrive late and leave their work to other volunteers.
options.explanation: This is wrong because the sentence describes registering for work, not arriving late.

options.text: They cancel their work plan and go home early.
options.explanation: This is wrong because the sentence describes joining a work period, not cancelling it.

options.text: They check tools for damage after the session ends.
options.explanation: This is wrong because checking tools describes the shift lead's task, not signing up.

exercises.explanation: In s3 the phrase means registering to work during a particular period.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that uses 'sign up for a shift' naturally and correctly.

options.text: I signed up for a shift on Saturday morning to help at the food bank.
options.explanation: This is correct because the verb form, article, and infinitive are all natural.

options.text: She sign up for a shift every weekend at the community clinic.
options.explanation: This is wrong because it should be signs up instead of sign up with She.

options.text: They signed up for a shift to helping at the shelter yesterday.
options.explanation: This is wrong because it should be to help instead of to helping.

options.text: We have signed up for shift on Friday evening at the library.
options.explanation: This is wrong because it should be for a shift instead of for shift.

exercises.explanation: Only one sentence uses the phrase with correct grammar and collocation.

exercises.prompt: In sentence s5 'If the café runs out of a common part, volunteers record the item,' what does 'runs out of' mean?

options.text: It orders more of the part before the stock becomes low.
options.explanation: This is wrong because ordering more happens after stock is gone, not the meaning itself.

options.text: It has no more of the part left because it has all been used.
options.explanation: This is correct because it paraphrases having nothing left after use.

options.text: It finds a replacement part in the labelled tray.
options.explanation: This is wrong because finding a part is different from having none left.

options.text: It repairs the part quickly for the waiting visitor.
options.explanation: This is wrong because repairing describes fixing, not having no stock left.

exercises.explanation: In s5 the phrase means having no more left after all has been used.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that uses 'runs out of' naturally and correctly.

options.text: The shop run out of milk yesterday afternoon and closed early.
options.explanation: This is wrong because it should be ran out instead of run out for yesterday.

options.text: Our office runs out of printer paper at the end of every month.
options.explanation: This is correct because the present simple form agrees with the routine meaning.

options.text: We runs out of bread every morning at the bakery counter.
options.explanation: This is wrong because it should be run instead of runs with We.

options.text: She runs out of time yesterday during the final test.
options.explanation: This is wrong because it should be ran out instead of runs out for yesterday.

exercises.explanation: Only one sentence uses the phrase with correct tense and subject agreement.

exercises.prompt: You are a roommate leaving a note for your housemate about kitchen supplies. Write 2–3 sentences explaining what is gone and what you will do next.
exercises.sampleAnswer: We ran out of cooking oil last night. I will buy a new bottle after class today.
selfCheck: I used a natural form of runs out of correctly.
I said what is gone and what I will do next.
